note: Every external claim that enters this tree passes through this file. Only entries with status 'verified' may support a claim. See corpus/README.md for the rule and corpus/validate_corpus.py for its enforcement.
verification_method: Each identifier was fetched from a machine-readable authority rather than recalled: the Europe PMC REST API (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:<pmid>&resultType=core), which returns the indexed title, authors, journal, DOI and abstract, or the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/<nct>) including the posted results section. 'verified_at' records the human-readable page for the same record. PubMed HTML pages and europepmc.org article pages were not usable (cookie wall and HTTP 403 respectively), which is why the APIs were used.

references.authors: Su Z, Kosillo P, Jung K, Chen S, Summers MT, Piet A, et al.
references.title: Topographic structure and function of locus coeruleus noradrenaline neurons
references.finding: Individual LC noradrenaline neurons have extensive but regionally confined axonal projections; projection target and graded gene expression correlate with cell-body position. Dorsal LC neurons projecting to isocortex activate on choice switches and carry reward-prediction-error signals; ventral LC background activity is higher when mice ignore reward-predicting stimuli.
references.caveat: Mouse. This is the published version of the preprint that experiments/influence/bounded-influence/theory/related.md cites as 'Su et al., Allen Institute, bioRxiv 717727', which that repo's PROVENANCE.md listed as not re-verified. The repo's description of the result is accurate; the citation was stale and is superseded by this one. Nothing here is a human result, so it licenses LC-NE as a candidate gain/noise mechanism, not as a demonstrated human knob.

references.authors: Clark KB, Naritoku DK, Smith DC, Browning RA, Jensen RA
references.title: Enhanced recognition memory following vagus nerve stimulation in human subjects
references.finding: Indexed as a Randomized Controlled Trial. Post-learning vagus nerve stimulation in epilepsy patients significantly enhanced word-recognition retention.
references.caveat: N=10. The foundation stone of the whole 'vagus stimulation improves memory' line, never replicated at scale. See clark1999-dose-numbers: the famous inverted-U figures attached to this paper are NOT verified.

references.authors: Ghacibeh GA, Shenker JI, Shenal B, Uthman BM, Heilman KM
references.title: The influence of vagus nerve stimulation on memory
references.finding: VNS vs sham in implanted epilepsy patients: no effect on learning, but enhanced consolidation and therefore improved retention.
references.caveat: N=10, overlapping research community with clark1999.

references.authors: Ghacibeh GA, Shenker JI, Shenal B, Uthman BM, Heilman KM
references.title: Effect of vagus nerve stimulation on creativity and cognitive flexibility
references.finding: Same cohort as ghacibeh2006-memory: VNS impaired cognitive flexibility (anagrams) and creativity (Torrance) while improving retention.
references.caveat: Load-bearing for honesty: the identical intervention in the identical subjects both helped and hurt, depending on the measure. 'VNS enhances cognition' is a selective reading of this literature.

references.authors: Frangos E, Ellrich J, Komisaruk BR
references.title: Non-invasive access to the vagus nerve central projections via electrical stimulation of the external ear: fMRI evidence in humans
references.finding: Cymba conchae stimulation vs earlobe: fMRI activation of ipsilateral nucleus tractus solitarius, spinal trigeminal nucleus, dorsal raphe and locus coeruleus.
references.caveat: The entire human mechanistic claim that taVNS reaches the LC rests on this single N=12 brainstem fMRI study. Brainstem fMRI at this N is a weak foundation for a causal chain, and the downstream markers it predicts are largely null (see pervaz2025-pupil-meta, contier2026-null).

references.authors: Keute M, Demirezen M, Graf A, Mueller NG, Zaehle T
references.title: No modulation of pupil size and event-related pupil response by transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation
references.finding: Randomized, single-blind, within-subject, earlobe sham. Null throughout: resting pupil chi2=1.3 p=0.254; time x stimulation chi2=0.1 p=0.738; event-related dilation chi2=0.5 p=0.468; tonic pupil during oddball chi2=2.6 p=0.108. Behaviour also null.
references.caveat: Indexed as a Randomized Controlled Trial. Authors used dAIC/dBIC and explicitly state this is not Bayesian inference, so this is a frequentist null rather than evidence for the null.

references.authors: Warren CM, Tona KD, Ouwerkerk L, van Paridon J, Poletiek F, van Steenbergen H, Bosch JA, Nieuwenhuis S
references.title: The neuromodulatory and hormonal effects of transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation as evidenced by salivary alpha amylase, salivary cortisol, pupil diameter, and the P3 event-related potential
references.finding: Across three experiments: P3 unaffected (Bayes factor favouring the null = 4.53); pupil unaffected (treatment x time p=.79); salivary alpha-amylase did increase and the cortisol decline was attenuated. Authors conclude taVNS modulates hormonal but not psychophysiological indices of noradrenergic function.
references.caveat: The one marker that moves (salivary alpha-amylase) is a peripheral sympathetic measure, not a central noradrenergic one.

references.authors: Burger AM, Van der Does W, Brosschot JF, Verkuil B
references.title: From ear to eye? No effect of transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation on human pupil dilation: a report of three studies
references.finding: No evidence that taVNS increases resting pupil diameter or task-related pupil dilation; no consistent effect on attentional-blink performance. Framed explicitly as a test of the LC-noradrenaline hypothesis, and a failed one.

references.authors: Contier F, Wartenburger I, Weymar M, Rabovsky M
references.title: No effect of continuous transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation on the P3, the P600, or physiological markers of noradrenergic activity
references.finding: Crossover, cymba vs earlobe. Robust P3 and P600 effects were present in the data, but taVNS modulated neither; salivary alpha-amylase and baseline pupil were also unaffected. Authors conclude the protocol may not have engaged LC-NE at all.
references.caveat: A positive control that worked (the ERPs were there) with a null manipulation is much stronger than a bare null.

references.authors: Pervaz I, Thurn L, Vezzani C, Kaluza L, Kuhnel A, Kroemer NB
references.title: Does transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation alter pupil dilation? A living Bayesian meta-analysis
references.finding: Overall g=0.15 [0.03, 0.27], BF01=1.0, inconclusive. Split by protocol: conventional/continuous taVNS g=0.002 [-0.14, 0.14], BF01=21.9, strong evidence FOR the null; pulsed/phasic taVNS g=0.36 [0.19, 0.53], BF10=50.8, strong evidence for an effect.
references.caveat: The single most informative number on taVNS mechanism. Note the preprint version (doi 10.1101/2024.09.02.610851) framed the same overall estimate as 'anecdotal evidence for the alternative'; the peer-reviewed version frames it as evidence for the null. Cite the published version only.

references.authors: Liu F, Li Y
references.title: Sorting the mind: cognitive enhancement through transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation - a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Pooled g=0.41 [0.30, 0.53], I2=51.4%. Executive function g=0.46; cognitive flexibility/learning g=0.53; working memory/attention g=0.19 [0.04, 0.33]; social cognition g=0.80 but k=3 and I2=82%.
references.caveat: The abstract reports no publication-bias or small-study-effect test (no funnel, Egger or trim-and-fill). A moderate pooled behavioural effect sitting on a largely null mechanism literature is the classic small-study-effect signature. Treat g=0.41 as an upper bound, not an estimate. Whether such a test appears in the full text was not checked.

references.authors: Giraudier M, Ventura-Bort C, Burger AM, Claes N, D'Agostini M, Warren CM, Weymar M, et al.
references.title: Evidence for a modulating effect of transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) on salivary alpha-amylase as indirect noradrenergic marker: a pooled mega-analysis
references.finding: Meta-analysis on summary statistics: no significant effect. Linear mixed models on pooled raw data: taVNS > sham, b=0.16, SE=0.05, p=0.001.
references.caveat: Analysis-dependent. The effect exists under one of two defensible analyses of the same data, which is a reason to discount it rather than to quote the significant one.

references.authors: Sharon O, Fahoum F, Nir Y
references.title: Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation in humans induces pupil dilation and attenuates alpha oscillations
references.finding: Short (3.4 s) phasic tVNS vs earlobe sham produced robust pupil dilation peaking at 4-5 s and greater alpha attenuation.
references.caveat: All-male sample. Phasic protocol: this is the arm that pervaz2025-pupil-meta finds does work, so it is consistent rather than contradictory with the continuous-protocol nulls.

references.authors: Ludwig M, Pereira C, Keute M, Duzel E, Betts MJ, Hammerer D
references.title: Evaluating phasic transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) with pupil dilation: the importance of stimulation intensity and sensory perception
references.finding: Phasic taVNS at higher intensity increased pupil dilation, but the effect attenuated once differences in perceived stimulation intensity were accounted for, and dilation scaled with perceived intensity.
references.caveat: Direct evidence that sham-control adequacy is a live threat: an arousal-from-sensation confound is not excluded for the phasic protocol either.

references.authors: Ventura-Bort C, Giraudier M, Weymar M
references.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation enhances emotional processing and long-term recognition memory: evidence across two studies
references.finding: Study 1 replicated the authors' own ERP findings (larger early LPP, larger late Old/New effect), but no effects of taVNS on memory performance were found.
references.caveat: A partial self-replication failure, and the cleanest illustration of the field's convergent-validity problem: the electrophysiology replicated and the behaviour did not.

references.authors: Mary A, Nematollahi H, Torres D, Chernyshkova Y, Vonck K, Carrette E
references.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation enhances episodic memory across valences and memory stages
references.finding: Randomized within-subject crossover across encoding, consolidation and retrieval with 24 h free recall: taVNS significantly enhanced recall vs sham. The largest healthy-volunteer taVNS memory study located.
references.caveat: Single-blind. Given that sham participants are 32.4% less likely to report unpleasant sensations, single-blind designs in this field do not fully control expectancy.

references.authors: Kaluza L, Kuhnel A, Gerth N, Wegner Y, Schulz C, Kroemer NB
references.title: Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation modulates Pavlovian bias in a state-dependent manner
references.finding: Single-blind randomized crossover, tVNS crossed with metabolic state. tVNS decreased Pavlovian Go x Win bias only after a caloric load (Stimulation x Load p=.038).
references.caveat: A borderline interaction, not a main effect. Hypothesis-generating. This is the closest published result to 'stimulation shifts a reinforcement-learning decision parameter in humans', and it is weak.

references.authors: Kotsaris V, Bolis D, Ozturk OC, Salaris A, Azevedo RT
references.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation modulates adaptive empathic learning under uncertainty
references.finding: Between-subjects active vs sham with hierarchical Gaussian filter modelling: no effect on accuracy or mean learning rates; effect only on learning-rate modulation between stable and volatile phases.
references.caveat: A second-order effect with primary outcomes null.

references.authors: Joshi S, Li Y, Kalwani RM, Gold JI
references.title: Relationships between pupil diameter and neuronal activity in the locus coeruleus, colliculi, and cingulate cortex
references.finding: LC activation reliably anticipates pupil changes, down to single spikes from single units. The paper's own conclusion is that this relationship is NOT specific to LC: similar relationships appear in inferior and superior colliculus and in anterior and posterior cingulate.
references.caveat: Routinely mis-cited as licensing 'pupil = LC'. It reports close to the opposite. Any document in this tree that cites it should be checked against this sentence.

references.authors: Megemont M, McBurney-Lin J, Yang H
references.title: Pupil diameter is not an accurate real-time readout of locus coeruleus activity
references.finding: A graded monotonic relation between LC spike count and pupil dilation exists, but with substantial variability: pupil accurately predicts only a small fraction of LC activity moment to moment, with large session-to-session variation in the pupil response to identical optogenetic LC stimulation. Pupil-LC coupling itself varies with brain state and decision bias.
references.caveat: Mouse. Together with joshi2016-pupil-lc this makes pupil a weak and non-specific LC proxy, which matters for any monitor in this tree that proposes to use arousal as a covariate.

references.authors: Aston-Jones G, Cohen JD
references.title: An integrative theory of locus coeruleus-norepinephrine function: adaptive gain and optimal performance
references.finding: Adaptive gain theory: phasic LC mode supports exploitation of the current task, tonic LC mode supports disengagement and exploration. NE acts as a gain parameter on decision dynamics.
references.caveat: A framework built on monkey neurophysiology plus modelling, never itself a human finding. Its one direct human pharmacological test found the effect in the opposite direction (warren2017-atomoxetine-exploration).

references.authors: Yu AJ, Dayan P
references.title: Uncertainty, neuromodulation, and attention
references.finding: Normative Bayesian account in which acetylcholine signals expected uncertainty and noradrenaline signals unexpected uncertainty, such as unsignalled context switches.
references.caveat: A normative model. Its best human support is marshall2016-pharma-fingerprints.

references.authors: Warren CM, Wilson RC, van der Wee NJ, Giltay EJ, van Noorden MS, Cohen JD, Nieuwenhuis S
references.title: The effect of atomoxetine on random and directed exploration in humans
references.finding: Double-blind crossover with atomoxetine (noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor). The effect fell on random and not directed exploration, as adaptive gain theory predicts, but atomoxetine REDUCED rather than increased random exploration: the opposite sign to the prediction.
references.caveat: N=22. A failed directional prediction of adaptive gain theory in humans. The authors offer three post-hoc explanations (inverted U, cross-neuromodulator interaction, phasic vs tonic); the inverted-U rescue is unfalsifiable until a dose-response design is run.

references.authors: Marshall L, Mathys C, Ruge D, de Berker AO, Dayan P, Stephan KE, Bestmann S
references.title: Pharmacological fingerprints of contextual uncertainty
references.finding: Noradrenergic, cholinergic and dopaminergic antagonism within one hierarchical Bayesian framework. Supports a noradrenergic role in learning from unexpected environmental changes; acetylcholine governs attribution of uncertainty to chance versus context violation.
references.caveat: The largest pharmacological test of the Yu and Dayan account located, and broadly consistent with it.

references.authors: de Gee JW, Kloosterman NA, Braun A, Donner TH
references.title: Catecholamines reduce choice history biases in perceptual decision making
references.finding: Atomoxetine decreased idiosyncratic choice-history bias, in either direction, relative to placebo; modelling attributes this to reduced bias in the evidence-accumulation process.
references.caveat: Has a published correction (PLoS Biology 23:e3003548, doi 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003548, PMID 41348660) which is cosmetic only: figure axis labels and missing ORCIDs. Conclusions unaffected.

references.authors: O'Callaghan C, Hezemans FH, Robbins TW, Rowe JB, et al.
references.title: Pharmacological and pupillary evidence for the noradrenergic contribution to reinforcement learning in Parkinson's disease
references.finding: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover, single-dose atomoxetine. Improved learning vs placebo; computational modelling located the change in the decision-noise parameter, a shift toward exploitation. Baseline pupil increased under atomoxetine and correlated with behavioural improvement.
references.caveat: N=19 patients. Clinical population, so does not transfer directly to healthy decision-making.

references.authors: Nuiten SA, de Gee JW, Zantvoord JB, Sterzer P, Fahrenfort JJ, van Gaal S
references.title: Phasic and tonic arousal distinctly shape human decision bias
references.finding: Pharmacology plus pupillometry plus EEG. Tonic pupil-linked arousal and pharmacological manipulation both produced more liberal decisions, but strategic bias shifts related to phasic pupil arousal and not to tonic pupil or to pharmacology.
references.caveat: A dissociation between the pharmacological and the pupillometric handle: they are not two windows on one variable, which matters for any design that treats pupil as a stand-in for a noradrenergic manipulation.

references.authors: University of Florida
references.title: Treatment of Mild Cognitive Impairment With Transcutaneous Vagal Nerve Stimulation
references.finding: COMPLETED, N=59 actual, DOUBLE masking (participant and investigator), randomized crossover with one-week washout, results posted. Primary outcome Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test total delayed recall: sham 6.43 vs tVNS 7.83, mixed-models beta=1.4, p=0.11. The prespecified primary endpoint was not met.
references.caveat: Registered primary purpose was BASIC_SCIENCE rather than efficacy, but it remains a prespecified primary outcome that did not reach significance. Independently re-fetched from the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 results section on 2026-10-20.

references.authors: Massachusetts General Hospital
references.title: The Wandering Nerve: Gateway to Boost Alzheimer's Disease Related Cognitive Performance
references.finding: COMPLETED (2021-11 to 2026-08), N=126 actual, single masking (participant), randomized crossover then placebo-controlled, stratified by APOE-e4. No results posted.
references.caveat: Its outcome is simply unknown. It must not be described as either positive or negative. The largest completed taVNS trial in this indication.

references.authors: Salzberg SL, White O, Peterson J, Eisen JA
references.title: Microbial genes in the human genome: lateral transfer or gene loss?
references.finding: An exciting cross-domain transfer claim dissolved once a proper null (gene loss plus rate variation plus sample-size effects) was applied.
references.caveat: Cited in experiments/influence/bounded-influence/theory/related.md purely as a methodological exemplar, not as domain support. Listed as not re-verified in that node's PROVENANCE.md; verified here.

references.authors: Clark KB, Naritoku DK, Smith DC, Browning RA, Jensen RA
references.title: The specific inverted-U dose figures attributed to Clark et al. 1999 (approx 35% enhancement at 0.5 mA, p<0.025; impairment at 0.75-1.5 mA)
references.why_unverified: The paper itself is verified (see clark1999-vns-memory, PMID 10195186). These specific numbers are NOT in the Europe PMC abstract, which states only that post-learning stimulation significantly enhanced retention. They appeared only in web search summaries. The DOI resolves to nature.com but the full text sits behind an authentication redirect and was not read. Do not quote the percentage, the p-value or the current levels without reading the PDF.

references.authors: unknown
references.title: Human studies of clonidine or guanfacine (alpha-2 adrenergic agonists) on exploration, learning rate or drift-diffusion decision parameters
references.why_unverified: Searched and not found. Targeted searches returned only reviews and unrelated work; no specific study could be verified. This is a genuine gap: either such studies are sparse, or the search missed them. Every noradrenergic-pharmacology result verified in this file uses atomoxetine or propranolol. Do not assume alpha-2 agonist evidence exists.

references.authors: Thompson LW, Joshi S, Gold JI
references.title: Limitations of pupil diameter as a proxy for modes of locus coeruleus activity
references.finding: Baseline and evoked relationships in pupil are not predictive of those in LC and vice versa; warns against inferring phasic versus tonic LC modes from pupil.
references.caveat: PREPRINT: no PMID, not peer-reviewed. Directly on point and pointing the same way as megemont2022-pupil-not-lc, but must be marked as a preprint at every use.

references.authors: Braak H, Thal DR, Ghebremedhin E, Del Tredici K
references.title: Stages of the pathologic process in Alzheimer disease: age categories from 1 to 100 years
references.venue: Journal of Neuropathology and Experimental Neurology 70:960-969
references.finding: 58 cases had subcortical tau predominantly in the locus coeruleus with no abnormal cortical tau; first amyloid-beta plaques appeared in neocortex after brainstem tauopathy onset.
references.caveat: Cross-sectional autopsy. The authors' own wording is hedged: tauopathy 'may begin ... possibly in the lower brainstem'. No one has watched tau travel in a living human.

references.authors: Braak H, Del Tredici K
references.title: The pathological process underlying Alzheimer's disease in individuals under thirty
references.finding: 38/42 had pretangle tau and 41/42 had no amyloid-beta. Of 26 lacking transentorhinal tau, 22 had subcortical lesions, and in 19 of those 22 the pretangle material was confined to the coeruleus/subcoeruleus complex.
references.caveat: Explicitly conditional: 'Assuming the pretangle alterations are not transient and do not regress'. If that assumption fails the inference fails.

references.authors: Ehrenberg AJ, Grinberg LT, et al.
references.title: Quantifying the accretion of hyperphosphorylated tau in the locus coeruleus and dorsal raphe nucleus
references.finding: Unbiased stereology: at Braak stage 0, 7.9% of LC neurons already carry hyperphosphorylated tau inclusions. LC inclusion-bearing neurons rose about 1.9-fold from Braak 0 to I (p=0.02), with no significant difference between Braak I and II.

references.authors: Theofilas P, Grinberg LT, et al.
references.title: Locus coeruleus volume and cell population changes during Alzheimer's disease progression
references.finding: LC volume falls 8.4% per Braak stage, but neuronal loss started only midway through AD progression and age-related changes spared the LC. Authors infer that a second trigger may be necessary.
references.caveat: Complicates the simple 'early LC tau causes early LC neuron loss' story: the tau is early, the cell loss is not.

references.authors: Lyness SA, Zarow C, Chui HC
references.title: Neuron loss in key cholinergic and aminergic nuclei in Alzheimer disease: a meta-analysis
references.finding: LC effect size d=2.28, but nucleus basalis d=2.48 across 33 studies (N=585) was larger. Dorsal raphe d=1.79, substantia nigra d=0.61.
references.caveat: Directly contradicts the common claim that the LC is the single hardest-hit nucleus in AD. Note it is in tension with Zarow et al. 2003 from the same group in the same year, which ranked LC above nucleus basalis.

references.authors: Wilson RS, Nag S, Boyle PA, Hizel LP, Yu L, Buchman AS, Schneider JA, Bennett DA
references.title: Neural reserve, neuronal density in the locus ceruleus, and cognitive decline
references.finding: Rush Memory and Aging Project, mean 5.8 years of annual testing on a 19-test battery. Higher neuronal density in every nucleus except VTA predicted slower cognitive decline, but with all nuclei modelled together only LC density remained (estimate 0.003, SE 0.001). Higher LC density attenuated the Lewy-body/cognition association.
references.caveat: The foundational datum for the whole 'LC as neural reserve' line, and the raw effect is very small. The exact p-value could not be read: the indexed abstract truncates it.

references.authors: Kelly SC, Counts SE, et al.
references.title: Locus coeruleus cellular and molecular pathology during the progression of Alzheimer's disease
references.n: 29 (11 no cognitive impairment, 10 amnestic MCI, 8 AD)
references.finding: 30% LC neuron loss from no-impairment to amnestic MCI and a further 25% in AD; loss tracked global cognition, episodic, semantic and working memory, perceptual speed and visuospatial ability.
references.caveat: The widely quoted '30% LC loss by MCI' figure rests on 11 versus 10 brains.

references.authors: Dahl MJ, Mather M, Duzel S, Bodammer NC, Lindenberger U, Kuhn S, Werkle-Bergner M
references.title: Rostral locus coeruleus integrity is associated with better memory performance in older adults
references.finding: Memory was positively associated with LC integrity in older adults (estimate 1.737, 95% CI 0.447-3.027).
references.caveat: The caveats are larger than the headline. Younger and older adults showed no reliable difference in average LC score (delta chi2=0.383, p=0.536); the rostral age difference was only a trend (cluster permutation p_corr=0.079); caudal LC intensity was significantly HIGHER in older adults (p_corr<0.001); and the memory-LC association failed to reach significance in younger adults. The 'rostral LC declines with age' framing is stronger than the statistics supporting it.

references.authors: Elman JA, et al.
references.title: MRI-assessed locus coeruleus integrity is heritable and associated with multiple cognitive domains, mild cognitive impairment, and daytime dysfunction
references.n: 481 men, ages 62-71.7 (Vietnam Era Twin Study of Aging)
references.finding: LC contrast-to-noise ratio heritability 0.48. Lower LC-CNR associated with poorer episodic memory, verbal and semantic fluency, processing speed, and higher odds of amnestic MCI.
references.caveat: Men only, narrow age band. Generalization unestablished.

references.authors: Jacobs HIL, Johnson KA, et al.
references.title: In vivo and neuropathology data support locus coeruleus integrity as indicator of Alzheimer's disease pathology and cognitive decline
references.finding: Lower LC integrity was associated with elevated entorhinal tau in unimpaired individuals. The largest-scale attempt to validate the in-vivo marker against pathology, and the strongest single support for it.
references.caveat: Its own key internal caveat: LC pigmentation ratings correlated with LC neuronal density but NOT with LC tangle density.

references.authors: Liu KY, Kievit RA, Tsvetanov KA, et al.
references.title: Noradrenergic-dependent functions are associated with age-related locus coeruleus signal intensity differences
references.finding: A pre-registered hypothesis that failed: the a priori two-factor model, in which LC relates separately to noradrenaline-dependent and noradrenaline-independent functions, fit WORSE than a unidimensional model in which LC related to a single general factor.
references.caveat: The data did not show the noradrenergic specificity that was predicted. The paper's positive framing is weaker than the pre-registration implied. This is the only pre-registered test in the LC-MRI aging literature located here, and it did not confirm specificity.

references.authors: Sibahi A, Cassidy CM, et al.
references.title: A longitudinal investigation of locus coeruleus-noradrenergic system integrity and cognitive performance across the Alzheimer's disease spectrum
references.venue: Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism 46:2623-2633
references.finding: The best longitudinal evidence located. Within-subject LC decline was significant only in early AD (t95=-3.72, p=0.0003) and not in later AD or in healthy aging. LC related to logical memory (t64=2.57, p=0.013) and object recognition (t64=3.41, p=0.001) in AD.
references.caveat: Single study, not replicated. Most of this literature is cross-sectional; this is the exception.

references.authors: Robertson IH
references.title: A noradrenergic theory of cognitive reserve: implications for Alzheimer's disease
references.finding: The actual origin of the LC cognitive-reserve hypothesis, frequently mis-attributed to Mather.
references.caveat: Explicitly framed by its author as 'a hypothesis' and 'a viable hypothesis', not an established mechanism.

references.authors: Mather M, Harley CW
references.title: The locus coeruleus: essential for maintaining cognitive function and the aging brain
references.finding: The canonical statement of the LC-protective line: noradrenaline released during arousing, novel or challenging situations helps protect neurons, proposed to explain why education and engaging careers delay decline.
references.caveat: A review, not evidence. Must be cited alongside mather2021-retreat, in which the same author substantially walks this back.

references.authors: Mather M
references.title: Noradrenaline in the aging brain: promoting cognitive reserve or accelerating Alzheimer's disease?
references.venue: Seminars in Cell and Developmental Biology 116:108-124
references.finding: The same author's substantial retreat from the one-sided protective framing: noradrenaline 'sometimes prevents and sometimes accelerates' amyloid-beta and tau production; mental stimulation 'may also have risks as well as benefits'; increased synaptic activity in older brains 'risks accelerating the accumulation of Alzheimer's pathology'.
references.caveat: Any unidirectional 'engage your LC to protect your brain' claim is unsupported, on the account of the person who proposed it.

references.authors: Mather M, Clewett D, Sakaki M, Harley CW
references.title: Norepinephrine ignites local hotspots of neuronal excitation: how arousal amplifies selectivity in perception and memory
references.finding: The GANE model: local glutamate signals representation strength and increases local noradrenaline release, forming hotspots where glutamate and noradrenaline mutually amplify, with widespread suppression elsewhere.
references.caveat: A theoretical synthesis. The 'noradrenaline hotspot' is a proposed mechanism, not an observed one.

references.authors: Sara SJ
references.title: Locus coeruleus reports changes in environmental contingencies
references.finding: The sharpest published criticism of GANE: 'careful perusal of the sparse data available from recording studies in animals' shows LC neurons are excited mainly by any environmental change, favouring a network-reset account over GANE.
references.caveat: The dispute is partly about whether the animal recording base is adequate to constrain either model at all.

references.authors: Heneka MT, et al.
references.title: Locus ceruleus controls Alzheimer's disease pathology by modulating microglial functions through norepinephrine
references.n: not stated in the indexed record
references.finding: LC degeneration in APP-transgenic mice raised inflammatory mediators and elevated amyloid-beta deposition, impaired microglial recruitment and phagocytosis, and was rescued by L-threo-DOPS. The foundational 'noradrenaline loss worsens amyloid' result.
references.caveat: Mouse. Sample size not stated in the record checked. Partly dissociated by evans2024-ne-inhibition, which found LC inhibition raised neuroinflammation WITHOUT altering amyloid.

references.authors: Rorabaugh JM, Chalermpalanupap T, Weinshenker D, et al.
references.title: Chemogenetic locus coeruleus activation restores reversal learning in a rat model of Alzheimer's disease
references.n: not stated in the indexed record
references.finding: In TgF344-AD rats, phosphorylated tau appeared in the LC before entorhinal cortex or hippocampus, and a Morris-water-maze reversal-learning deficit was rescued by DREADD-mediated LC activation.
references.caveat: Rat, and CHEMOGENETIC, not optogenetic: the optogenetic version of this result could not be found and should not be cited (see optogenetic-lc-ad-rescue). Short-term stimulation. Compare nong2026-chronic-stim-worse, where long-term stimulation reverses the sign.

references.authors: Chalermpalanupap T, Weinshenker D, et al.
references.title: Locus coeruleus ablation exacerbates cognitive deficits, neuropathology, and lethality in P301S tau transgenic mice
references.n: not stated in the indexed record
references.finding: DSP-4 lesion from 2 months produced spatial and contextual memory deficits by 6 months only in lesioned P301S mice, with exacerbated neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration and accelerated mortality by 10 months.
references.caveat: The authors found only 'a mild aggravation of tau pathology', so increased tau cannot fully account for the effect. The mechanism is therefore not established.

references.authors: Nong Y, Wang Q, et al.
references.title: Long-term locus coeruleus stimulation exacerbates tau pathology in PS19 mice
references.n: not stated in the indexed record
references.finding: Direct counter-evidence to 'stimulate the LC to treat Alzheimer's'. Chronic chemogenetic LC stimulation worsened spatial memory, impaired contextual fear memory, reduced hippocampal long-term potentiation, and increased tau hyperphosphorylation and neuroinflammation. The paper explicitly contrasts itself with the short-term TgF344-AD rescue.
references.caveat: Mouse. Duration of stimulation flips the sign of the effect. Any proposal to use LC drive as a behavioural or therapeutic lever must specify duration and dose before claiming a direction.

references.authors: Evans AK, Shamloo M, et al.
references.title: Impact of noradrenergic inhibition on neuroinflammation and pathophysiology in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease
references.finding: Chemogenetic LC inhibition and beta-blockade both potentiated neuroinflammation without altering amyloid-beta pathology, dissociating the inflammation and amyloid arms of the Heneka account. Microglial adrb2 deletion helped in females only; adrb1 deletion did nothing.
references.caveat: Authors conclude non-microglial cell types likely mediate the effect, so the canonical microglial mechanism is not secure.

references.authors: Levey AI, Weinshenker D, et al.
references.title: A phase II study repurposing atomoxetine for neuroprotection in mild cognitive impairment
references.n: 39 participants with MCI and AD biomarkers
references.finding: Double-blind crossover over 12 months. Target engagement was achieved (plasma and CSF noradrenaline rose). Both pre-specified primary outcomes failed: IL-1alpha and TECK were not measurable in most samples. There were no significant treatment effects on cognition or clinical outcomes. CSF tau and pTau181 were reduced versus placebo as secondary or exploratory findings; amyloid-beta 42 was unchanged.
references.caveat: The only noradrenaline-augmentation trial in this indication located. Small, single-centre, and its positive findings are secondary or exploratory. It is not evidence that boosting noradrenaline improves cognition in MCI.

references.authors: Bachman SL, Mather M, et al.
references.title: Daily heart rate variability biofeedback training decreases locus coeruleus MRI contrast in younger adults in a randomized clinical trial
references.n: younger and older adults; N not stated in the indexed record
references.finding: Five weeks of slow paced breathing reduced left LC contrast in younger participants, in proportion to how much they increased heart-rate oscillations, and the decrease tracked reduced CREB-associated gene expression. No effect in older participants.
references.caveat: Among the most damaging results for the field's core assumption. If a five-week breathing intervention moves 'LC structural integrity', the measure is not purely structural.

references.authors: Keren NI, Eckert MA, et al.
references.title: Histologic validation of locus coeruleus MRI contrast in post-mortem tissue
references.finding: The study the entire in-vivo LC-MRI field cites as its histological validation. It concluded that LC-MRI contrast corresponds to neuromelanin cell location.
references.caveat: The authors themselves wrote that there were too few tissue samples (n=7) to perform correlational analyses, and that there was a wide range of LC-MRI contrast within and across samples that appeared unrelated to age. The foundational validation is n=7 with no correlational test.

references.authors: Watanabe T, Tan Z, Wang X, Martinez-Hernandez A, Frahm J
references.title: Magnetic resonance imaging of noradrenergic neurons
references.finding: Direct challenge to the term 'neuromelanin-sensitive'. High LC magnetization-transfer signal was present in 3-week-old mice and in DBH-knockout mice, and rodents largely lack neuromelanin; there was no correlation between MTR/R1 and iron, copper or manganese in human brain. The authors attribute the signal to abundant water protons whose T1 is shortened by paramagnetic ions in active cells. The signal was absent in Ear2-knockout mice lacking noradrenaline neurons, so it does index noradrenergic cell bodies, but possibly via cellular activity rather than pigment accumulation.
references.caveat: If the signal is an activity marker rather than a pigment-accumulation marker, 'LC integrity' means something different from what most papers using it assume.

references.authors: Trujillo P, Zecca L, Costa A, et al.
references.title: Contrast mechanisms associated with neuromelanin-MRI
references.finding: Metal-free melanin had a negligible effect on magnetization-transfer spectra. Contrast arises from melanin-iron complexes shortening T1, not from melanin itself.
references.caveat: So 'neuromelanin-sensitive' contrast is in substantial part an iron measure.

references.authors: Tona KD, van Osch MJP, et al.
references.title: In vivo visualization of the locus coeruleus in humans: quantifying the test-retest reliability
references.finding: Two sessions about 2.8 months apart: intra-rater Dice 0.65-0.74, inter-rater Dice 0.54-0.64 ('moderate'), contrast ICC 0.63 for ROI and 0.53 for max-intensity.
references.caveat: An ICC of 0.53 is poor. The authors' own conclusion is that clinical or longitudinal studies should be carried out carefully.

references.authors: Dmitrichenko O, Draganski B, et al.
references.title: The quest for the best: manual, atlas- and spatial prior-based delineation of locus coeruleus
references.finding: Seven open-access LC atlases showed spatial concordance of only Dice 0.2-0.4. Mean inter-rater Dice was about 0.7, and the best voxel-wise similarity of probabilistic priors to manual labelling was r=0.3. In the 2393-participant cohort, LC volume followed an inverted-U trajectory across adulthood rather than monotonic decline.
references.caveat: The field cannot agree where the LC is. Any cross-study comparison of 'LC integrity' is comparing partly different pieces of brainstem.

references.authors: Liu KY, Hammerer D, et al.
references.title: In vivo visualization of age-related differences in the locus coeruleus
references.finding: LC contrast ratio versus age is quadratic, peaking around age 60: LC signal rises through midlife before falling. Age-related decline was confined to rostral LC, with greater variance in older adults and no sex difference.
references.caveat: Largest single LC-MRI aging sample located. The non-monotonic shape complicates any reading of LC contrast as cumulative neuron loss. See liu2020-corrigendum.

references.authors: Liu KY, et al.
references.title: Corrigendum to 'In vivo visualization of age-related differences in the locus coeruleus'
references.finding: The LC Cam-CAN mask spatial overlap relative to the Betts mask should be 51%, not 19% as reported, due to a data analysis coding error; and a supplementary mask file should not be used as it is a mislabeled version of another group's mask, uploaded in error. Main conclusions stated to be unaffected.
references.caveat: Even after correction, two leading published LC masks overlap only 51%. Concrete evidence of the spatial-definition problem in the field's own words.

references.authors: Liu KY, Marijatta F, Hammerer D, Acosta-Cabronero J, Duzel E, Howard RJ
references.title: Magnetic resonance imaging of the human locus coeruleus: a systematic review
references.finding: Structural studies consistently show lower LC signal or volume in clinical groups, but reported functional LC location coordinates were widely distributed compared with previously published neuroanatomical locations.
references.caveat: Many published 'LC' functional activations may not be LC.

references.authors: Betts MJ, et al.
references.title: Locus coeruleus imaging as a biomarker for noradrenergic dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases
references.finding: The field's own consensus statement, from roughly 30 authors. Framed entirely prospectively: LC imaging 'could help', 'holds the promise', and the paper outlines 'next steps ... to evaluate the potential'.
references.caveat: The field's own experts did not, in 2019, claim LC imaging was a validated biomarker. Seven years later dmitrichenko2026-atlas-disagreement shows the harmonisation steps they called for have not been met.

references.authors: unknown
references.title: Locus coeruleus or noradrenergic neuron transplantation as an intervention in Alzheimer's disease models
references.why_unverified: Searched and not found. Europe PMC queries for LC grafting/transplantation returned two hits, neither in an AD model (an intraocular transplant study and a 1990 study grafting LC neurons into adult rat hippocampus); a query combining noradrenergic transplantation with Alzheimer or amyloid returned zero hits. LC grafting into normal rat hippocampus is real; LC transplantation as an AD-model intervention could not be confirmed to exist. Do not cite such a paper without a specific PMID.

references.authors: unknown
references.title: Optogenetic locus coeruleus stimulation improving memory in an Alzheimer's disease model
references.why_unverified: Searched and not found. A query combining optogenetic, locus coeruleus and Alzheimer returned zero hits; the optogenetic LC work located was in normal rats and mice. The AD-model causal rescue result that does exist is CHEMOGENETIC (see rorabaugh2017-chemogenetic). Do not attribute it to optogenetics.

references.authors: unknown
references.title: A meta-analysis of LC MRI as an Alzheimer's disease biomarker
references.why_unverified: The only AD-relevant hit for an LC-MRI meta-analysis is a conference abstract with no listed authors, no PMID and no DOI. Not citable. The verified meta-analysis in this file (lyness2003-meta) is of autopsy cell counts, not MRI.

references.authors: Novelli L, Stoliker D, Barta T, Greaves MD, Chopra S, Jackson J, Kwee J, Pang JC, Williams ML, Razi A
references.title: PsiConnect: Multimodal Neuroimaging of Context-Dependent Brain and Behaviour Dynamics under Psilocybin
references.finding: A multimodal dataset: 62 participants scanned before and after a single 19 mg oral dose of psilocybin, with multi-echo fMRI, structural and diffusion MRI and EEG, across resting state and three naturalistic conditions (guided meditation, music, movie). Half the cohort completed an 8-week meditation training programme, so set and setting are crossed with drug. A full behavioural and self-report battery with follow-ups.
references.caveat: This is the dataset paper, not a result. It is what experiments/influence/bounded-influence/theory/related.md cites as its ground-truth barrier-lowering testbed; that node's PROVENANCE.md listed the citation as not re-verified, and it is now verified. The dataset's value to this tree is that it is a rare case of an experimentally controlled manipulation of the quantity the model calls barrier height, with brain and behaviour recorded.

references.authors: Cooper G, Stoliker D, Astl Delgado SV, Blackburne G, Novelli L, Green DW, Razi A, Das RK, Skipper JI
references.title: Language-associated brain representations covary with disruption of selfhood under psilocybin
references.n: 43 with ego-dissolution scores, 49 with imagery scores, 50 paired resting scans, from the 62-person PsiConnect cohort
references.finding: Under psilocybin, the component cluster whose inter-subject representational similarity tracked ego dissolution was a left-lateralised frontotemporal network whose map matched the Neurosynth language map at r=0.382 (spatial-null p<0.001, q=0.003), nearly twice the best comparator (imagery r=0.208; baseline r<=0.12). A connectivity score seeded on that cluster correlated with ego dissolution at rho=0.455 (Bonferroni-adjusted p=0.048) and not with imagery (rho=0.008); item-level, the loss-of-ego and loss-of-identity items correlated at rho about 0.43-0.51. Inter-subject correlation during music FELL under psilocybin, so a global rise in stimulus tracking does not explain the convergence.
references.caveat: PREPRINT, not peer-reviewed, posted 2026-10-14, no PMID. Its own stated limits are the load-bearing ones here: language involvement is REVERSE INFERENCE from meta-analytic maps with no direct measure of language or inner speech; the ego-dissolution scale was completed once after scanning, so it is retrospective; resting-state seeds came from the same participants, so it needs independent replication; and the authors explicitly flag ERGODICITY - between-person associations may not hold within individuals. That last caveat is this tree's own claim 2 appearing in someone else's data.
